title: Sepia & Script — Quarterly Family Letter
description: A warmly intimate family newsletter built around a three-image candid photo strip and a dusty-rose script greeting. Distinguished from holiday-card templates by its editorial body serif and a handwritten closing that signals a real person composed it.
philosophy: This design believes updates shared across generations should feel like a folded letter pulled from an envelope, not a branded content piece. It prioritizes warmth over polish — gently imperfect photo proportions, a script headline that mimics handwriting, and a signed-off closing that carries personal weight. It firmly rejects corporate type hierarchy, promotional color blocking, and any visual element that could be mistaken for marketing. It belongs to the speaker who prints it and mails it, not the one who exports it to a pitch deck.
goodFor: Quarterly family roundup newsletters sent to grandparents or extended family
Holiday life-update letters featuring candid children's photos
Printed or emailed personal milestone announcements (first day of school, new home)
Intimate one-page family bulletins where a handwritten sign-off feels appropriate
avoidFor: Corporate or brand communications requiring professional visual authority
Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews or data presentations
Slide decks with multiple sections needing strong typographic hierarchy
Social media promotional graphics where script headlines lose legibility at small sizes
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like the front face of a letter someone folded by hand — unhurried, warm, and faintly sun-faded at the edges. A flowing script greeting commands the composition with the intimacy of handwriting, carrying personal weight rather than typographic authority. Three candid snapshots nestle beneath it like photographs tucked into a correspondence envelope, warm-toned and gently imperfect in their framing. Avoid any visual sharpness, symmetrical grid precision, or promotional energy — nothing here should look designed; it should look composed by a person, not a brand.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with generous outer margins (~10%) evoking stationery whitespace, giving the slide the quiet breathing room of a printed letter. The script greeting dominates the upper-center zone across roughly columns 2–11, serving as the single expressive headline with no competing elements above it. A horizontal three-image candid photo strip anchors the lower half, with images allowed slightly uneven crop heights to signal organic, non-editorial curation. A brief serif identifier — family name, season, or year — sits below the strip, right-aligned to col 10, with no rule lines, header bands, or page numbers interrupting the surrounding negative space.

examples.promptCore: Feels like a letter composed unhurriedly at a kitchen table — warm, slightly imperfect, unmistakably personal. The three candid photos carry emotional weight without demanding symmetry; they read as a loose horizontal sequence, not a curated mood board. Body copy settles into an editorial rhythm that is serious enough to carry real news yet never institutional or promotional. The handwritten closing is the emotional anchor of the entire slide — it signals a real author, real care, and a piece of correspondence that belongs in a drawer, not a brand deck.

examples.layoutNotes: Single-column editorial layout with a generous 9% outer margin on each side; a three-image candid photo strip spans the full text measure as a horizontal band near the upper third, each frame allowed slightly uneven proportions for an organic, non-grid feel. A script-style section greeting floats above the strip, separated by open whitespace rather than a rule line or color band. Body copy runs below as one relaxed full-width column, broken only by a soft midpoint rest. A handwritten-style sign-off sits flush-left at the base with no footer band, page number, or decorative border beneath it.
